record iPhone sales and an all-time high in Services.\n- Diluted EPS -- $2.10, rising 14% and including a $0.05 favorable impact from tariff refunds.\n- iPhone Revenue -- $57.6 billion, growing 17% despite supply constraints and foreign exchange headwinds.\n- Services Revenue -- $31.6 billion, up 10% and reaching an all-time record led by video, cloud, and payment services.\n- Mac Revenue -- $10.8 billion, a 24% increase fueled by demand for the MacBook Neo and MacBook Pro models.\n- iPad Revenue -- $6.2 billion, declining 10% due to supply constraints and a difficult comparison against the prior year's A16-powered iPad launch.\n- Wearables, Home and Accessories Revenue -- $8.3 billion, down 8% reflecting a difficult comparison against the previous year's Watch SE 3 and AirPods Pro 3 releases.\n- Company Gross Margin -- 47.9%, benefiting by 1 percentage point from tariff refunds but offset by higher memory costs.\n- Services Gross Margin -- 76.0%, increasing 40 basis points sequentially.\n- Operating Expenses -- $19.2 billion, rising 21% primarily due to increased investments in research and development for artificial intelligence.\n- Active Installed Base -- Over 2.5 in share repurchases and $3.9 billion in dividends and equivalents.\n- Manufacturing Purchase Obligations -- $33 billion increase from the June quarter to the September quarter, reflecting efforts to secure supply.\n- Quarterly Net Income -- $30.7 billion, setting a September quarter record even when excluding tariff refund benefits.\n- December Quarter Revenue Guidance -- 7% to 10% growth, representing management's best view of constrained supply during the holiday season.\n- December Quarter Services Guidance -- 8% to 9% growth, contemplating sequential headwinds from third-party licensing and foreign exchange.\n- December Quarter Gross Margin Guidance -- 45% to 46%, reflecting the impact of higher memory costs and Siri AI ramp expenses.\n- Regional Performance -- 21% growth in Greater China, driven by record iPhone sales and strong performance in the Mac segment.\n\nNeed a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? (AAPL -1.87%) reported record September quarter results driven by double-digit growth in iPhone and Mac revenue alongside an all-time high for its Services division. Management reported that the company achieved its best fiscal year for both revenue and earnings per share, supported by an active installed base that now exceeds 2.5 billion devices. The company stated that it is currently navigating significant macroeconomic and supply chain challenges, specifically citing unprecedented memory pricing and constraints on advanced semiconductor nodes. We expect this to be the best quarter for revenue in the history of the company. We expect services revenue to grow between 8% and 9% year-over-year in the December quarter. This contemplates sequential headwinds, primarily driven by third-party licensing and foreign exchange. We expect gross margin to be between 45% and 46%.\n\nThis includes primarily the impact of higher memory costs as well as some costs related to the ramp of Siri AI. With that, I'll hand it back to John.\n\n...\n\nJohn Ternus: Yes. Let me give you an overall view on memory. What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented. And as we said earlier in the September quarter, we did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which were partly offset by the benefit of carrying inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components. Now for the December quarter, we expect even higher memory costs, partly offset by a few factors. So as you know, we changed the price on many of our products, including Mac and iPad at the end of June and iPhone in September, and these price increases provided some offset.\n\nWe also expect to see some benefit from carry-in inventory in the December quarter as well, as well as lower costs on certain non-memory components. And looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase. As we've said before, we do believe we'll see a decreasing benefit from the carry-in inventory on memory over time. So as we continue to roll out Siri AI to more customers, the associated cloud costs will be recognized through services cost of sales. And consistent with how we've always accounted for Mac, Siri and iCloud for the devices we sell that include these bundled services, we defer a portion of the revenue and recognize it over the life of the device. So our hardware deferrals as of the December quarter will reflect the addition of Siri AI. Both of these items will have an impact to the gross margin.\n\nBut as always, we look to continue to make the investments necessary to support the business. And we also see a wide range of ways that AI can contribute to revenue growth over time. So on the product side, we feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities. And we also feel there's opportunities across third-party apps and partnerships as well as first-party opportunities, as John highlighted earlier, with the expanded access to server side features of Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features as well.\n\n...\n\nSabih Khan: Yes. But as we have transitioned more of our lineup to the latest 2-nanometer technology nodes, our constraints on advanced nodes are easing. The company said quarterly revenue rose 12% from a year earlier, while diluted EPS increased 14%. Even so, the stock fell 2.8% in after-hours trading to $328.85, extending a 1.83% decline in the regular session, as investors weighed record sales against pressure from memory costs, supply constraints and heavier spending on artificial intelligence.\n\n## Key Takeaways\n\n- Apple beat expectations on both profit and revenue, but the stock fell after hours.\n- Quarterly revenue reached $114.5 billion, a September-quarter record.\n- iPhone, Mac and services all posted strong growth, helping drive a record fiscal year.\n- Gross margin held at 47.9%, but management warned that memory costs remain a major headwind.\n- The company guided for another record revenue quarter in the December period, but with margin pressure.\n\n## Company Performance\n\nApple said fiscal 2026 was its best year ever, with revenue of $478.8 billion, up 15% from the prior year, and EPS of $8.98, up 20%. Net income in the September quarter reached a record $30.7 billion. Operating cash flow totaled $28.1 billion.\n\nThe company’s core businesses remained strong. iPhone revenue rose 17% to $57.6 billion, Mac revenue increased 24% to $10.8 billion, and services revenue climbed 10% to a record $31.6 billion. Apple said its active installed base topped 2.5 billion devices across all major product categories.\n\nThe results came despite nearly 2 percentage points of foreign-exchange headwinds and supply constraints across iPhone, Mac and iPad. That combination makes the quarter look even stronger, though it also helps explain why investors did not reward the stock more aggressively.\n\n## Financial Highlights\n\n- Revenue: $114.48 billion, up 12% year over year.\n- EPS: $2.10, up 14% year over year.\n- Net income: $30.7 billion, a September-quarter record.\n- Fiscal 2026 revenue: $478.8 billion, up 15% year over year.\n- Fiscal 2026 EPS: $8.98, up 20% year over year.\n- Gross margin: 47.9%.\n- Products gross margin: 37.2%.\n- Services gross margin: 76%, up 40 basis points sequentially.\n- Operating cash flow: $28.1 billion.\n- Capital returned to shareholders: $28 billion, including $24 billion in share repurchases and $3.9 billion in dividends and equivalents.\n\n## Earnings vs. Forecast\n\nApple’s EPS beat of $0.11 per share, or 5.53%, was modest but clear. Revenue beat estimates by $1.10 billion, or 0.97%. The profit surprise was more meaningful than the sales surprise, suggesting the company managed costs and mix better than expected.\n\nThe quarter was also strong relative to Apple’s own recent trend. Revenue rose 12% year over year, faster than many large-cap technology peers, and the company posted records for quarterly revenue, net income and fiscal-year sales. Still, the beat was not large enough to change the broader debate around margins, memory inflation and supply limits.\n\n## Market Reaction\n\nApple shares closed the regular session at $338.32, down 1.83% from $344.63 the previous day. After the earnings release, the stock fell further to $328.85, down 2.8% from the close and about 4.6% below the prior day’s finish.\n\nThe shares remain close to the top of their 52-week range of $243.42 to $351.73, but the post-earnings drop suggests investors were looking beyond the headline beat. The reaction points to concern about near-term gross margin pressure, especially from memory costs, and about the costs tied to Apple’s AI rollout. No unusual volume data was provided.\n\n## Outlook & Guidance\n\nApple said it expects December-quarter revenue to rise 7% to 10% from a year earlier, which would make it the best quarter in company history. Services revenue is expected to grow 8% to 9%.\n\nGross margin is expected to come in between 45% and 46%, with management saying most of the sequential decline from the September quarter should come from higher memory costs. The company also said Siri AI rollout costs will flow through services cost of sales, while hardware deferrals will reflect the addition of Siri AI.\n\nOperating expenses are expected to be between $20.4 billion and $20.8 billion, up 11% to 13% from a year earlier, driven by continued investment in research and development, especially AI. Apple said its tax rate should be about 17%. Despite near-term margin pressures, InvestingPro assigns Apple a Financial Health score of 3.08 out of 5, rated as \"GREAT,\" reflecting the company’s strong return on assets of 36% and robust cash generation. This is an amazing time at Apple. We just completed one of the most prolific launch periods in our history. It's been a remarkable time for innovation across all of our categories. One of the greatest testaments to that is the all-new iPhone Duo, the most transformational iPhone since the original.\n\n We're also incredibly excited about iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, which take massive leaps forward on camera, battery life, and performance, features that our users care deeply about. Meanwhile, touch has arrived on Mac for the first time with the all-new MacBook Pro, and we were excited to announce the new iMac and 14-inch MacBook Pro. The all-new iPad mini features a stunning new OLED display and brings a super-thin design to the smallest member of the iPad family. Apple Watch now offers users the clearest window yet into their heart health. We introduced AirPods 5, which feature industry-leading active noise cancellation in an open-ear design. And we've laid the foundation for an even more intelligent smart home with the all-new HomeView, Apple TV 4K, and HomePod mini.\n\n On top of it all, we're unlocking more powerful AI experiences across our lineup, including with the all-new Siri AI, a profoundly capable and deeply personal assistant seamlessly integrated across our platforms. Like everything we make, Siri AI is built with essential privacy protections, so no one can access users' data, not even Apple. We launched Siri AI in beta for U.S. English users in September and expanded to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish in October. We're really excited to have rolled all these innovations out, and there's still so much more we plan to do. I'm feeling great about the opportunities ahead for Apple, from our product roadmap and broad range of services to promising areas like health, emerging markets, enterprise, and education. As one example, we recently secured our biggest education deal ever for Mac with the Department of Education in the Philippines.\n\n They're going to deploy 170,000 MacBook Neos to teachers and staff. Opportunities like this bring more users into our ecosystem and help fuel growth across our business. Apple is the greatest company in the world. We've assembled an extraordinary collection of talent, the best engineers, designers, developers, and experts in every corner of our business, from our supply chain to our stores. Every day, we bring the right people together with the best ideas to build products and services that change lives, guided by a foundational set of values and a belief that the best technology should make a better world. What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented. As we said earlier in the September quarter, we did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which were partly offset by the benefit of carry-in inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components. Our hardware deferrals as of the December quarter will reflect the addition of Siri AI. Both of these items will have an impact to the gross margin. Obviously, on-device is very, very efficient, no real cost associated with that.\n\n But on the server side, we would have some inference costs, and that is really the connection of the Siri AI-related costs that I mentioned that would be recognized with services cost of sales. Cash and returns: $137B in cash and marketable securities; $80B total debt; $28B returned to shareholders in the quarter (dividends and buybacks: $3.9B dividends, $24B buybacks).\n  - Dividend: $0.27 per share payable Nov 16, 2026; record date Nov 12, 2026.\n\n- Key factors influencing December outlook:\n  - Memory costs: expected to be higher, contributing to margin pressure.\n  - Product pricing actions: price increases on Mac, iPad (June), and iPhone (September) offset some margin headwinds.\n  - Carry-in inventory: potential offset to some extent; plus some cost reductions on certain non-memory components.\n  - Tariffs and macro backdrop: outlook assumes current tariff rates/policies remain and no worsening macro conditions.\n\n- Siri AI and product strategy:\n  - Introduction of all-new Siri AI across platforms, with privacy protections; beta in the U.S. English market launched in September, expanded to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish in October.\n  - Emphasis on AI features as a growth vector across devices, services, health, enterprise, and education.\n\n- Leadership tone:\n  - Confidence in opportunities ahead driven by product roadmap, services, health, emerging markets, enterprise, and education.\n  - Positive near-term growth expectations despite margin pressure from memory costs and AI-related ramp.\n\nBottom-line takeaway for December quarter: Revenue growth of 7–10% YoY, driven by services and overall demand, with gross margins pressured to 45–46% due to higher memory costs and AI investments, while the company continues to deploy capital and expand AI capabilities like Siri AI.","image":"https://stockanalysis.com/stockanalysis-1200x630.png"},{"id":"https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/03/apple-earnings-john-ternus-faces-first-test-amid-high-memory-costs.html","title":"Apple earnings: John Ternus faces first test amid high memory costs","url":"https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/03/apple-earnings-john-ternus-faces-first-test-amid-high-memory-costs.html","publishedDate":"2026-11-03T00:00:00.000Z","author":"Kif Leswing","text":"Apple earnings: John Ternus faces first test amid high memory costs\n\n# Apple stock sinks as global memory crisis hurts profits, giving Ternus his first big test\n\nPublished Tue, Nov 3 2026 7:00 AM EST Updated Tue, Nov 3 2026 9:38 AM EST\n\nKif Leswing@kifleswing\n\nKey Points\n\n- In John Ternus' first earnings report as CEO, Apple issued a gross margin forecast that disappointed Wall Street, sending the stock down after hours. \n- Apple blamed higher memory prices and some costs related to Siri AI for the shrinking margins. \n- \"Looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase,\" Ternus said. \n\nApple CEO John Ternus delivers a keynote address during the Apple Experience LA event in Los Angeles, California, on Oct. 28, 2026, introducing new Mac computer models. \n\nFrederic J. Brown | AFP | Getty Images\n\nJohn Ternus' first earnings report as Apple Add To Watchlist CEO was going fine until it was time to issue a forecast for the company's gross margin, one of the key metrics followed by investors. \n\nApple reported better-than-expected earnings and revenue on Monday, including in the company's core iPhone unit, and even projected sales in the current period that topped estimates. But just before Ternus opened the earnings call up to analysts' questions, CFO Kevan Parekh came forward with the first real piece of bad news. \n\nParekh said that for the December quarter, which goes through the holiday season, Apple's gross margin will be between 45% and 46%, trailing the 46.3% average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. \n\n\"This includes primarily the impact of higher memory costs, as well as some costs related to the ramp of Siri AI,\" Parekh said.\n\nApple shares slid 3% in morning trading on Tuesday.\n\nApple stock chart\n\nIt's part of an ongoing trend for Apple, which is absorbing some of the soaring costs from the global memory shortage. A margin drop in the fiscal first quarter would be a third straight decline for Apple, following a gross margin of 50.1% in the June period and 47.9% in the September quarter, boosted by 1 percentage point of tariff refunds. \n\nAt the midpoint of the forecast range, it would be Apple's lowest gross margin since the fiscal fourth quarter of 2023. \n\n\"What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented,\" Ternus said on the call, adding that the company is paying more than it did earlier this year. \"Looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase.\" \n\nTernus, who took the reins from Tim Cook on Sept. 1, is grappling with a problem that his predecessor spent his final months addressing. Cook told The Wall Street Journal in June that the memory situation was a \"hundred-year flood.\" Apple followed by raising prices across the board on Macs, iPads and accessories. \n\nIn September, Apple increased the prices of its iPhones by $100, which Ternus said the company did \"reluctantly.\"\n\n## 'Less flexibility in the supply chain'\n\nComputer and smartphone makers everywhere are suffering. On Friday, Intel Add To Watchlist had its worst day on the market since the 1970s due to a weak forecast tied to the softening PC market. It's all because of insatiable artificial intelligence demand.\n\nAI server giants like Nvidia Add To Watchlist and hyperscalers are buying up all the RAM they can find, and they're willing to pay a premium for it, leaving little supply for companies that make smartphones and tablets.\n\nDespite its size and global clout, Apple said it expects supply constraints on iPhones and Macs in the holiday quarter, primarily driven by memory. \n\nOn the call, Ternus had some top lieutenants field component-related questions. Sabih Khan, chief operating officer, became the first Apple COO to appear on an earnings call since Cook in 2010, when Steve Jobs was CEO. \n\n\"As we have said before, we're seeing less flexibility in the supply chain than normal,\" Khan told analysts on the call. \n\nIn response, Apple has drastically increased its purchase obligations to secure supply, Khan said. Those obligations rose by $33 billion from the June quarter to the September period, Khan said, though he declined to answer questions about whether Apple had signed \"long-term agreements\" with memory makers. \n\n\"We're always working hard to improve supply,\" Khan said.\n\nEven with the recent margin slide, Apple's gross margins are still well above where they sat earlier in the Cook era, when the number would predictably come in between 38% and 39%. As Apple's profitable services business grew, its gross margin expanded, hitting 40% in 2021 and growing from there.\n\nAnalysts see a potential silver lining for Apple in the current market turmoil. Because Apple is more capable of eating a portion of the increased costs, some experts predict the company will take market share from makers of Windows PC and Android phones that don't have such a cushion. \n\nCiting data from a third-party researcher, Ternus said gains are already happ","highlights":["said that for the December quarter, which goes through the holiday season, Apple's gross margin will be between 45% and 46%, trailing the 46.3%\n...\nThis includes primarily the impact of higher memory costs, as well as some costs related to the ramp of"],"summary":"Apple Q4 2026 earnings (call dated Nov 2, 2026) - Key takeaways\n\n- Management commentary focused on margin pressure from higher memory costs and ramp-related costs.\n- December quarter (holiday quarter) outlook: gross margin guidance of 45% to 46%, below the prior period’s 46.3%.\n- Commentary highlights: impact from elevated memory costs and costs tied to ramping certain products or initiatives. Here are the details.\n\n## Apple’s gross margins fall despite record revenue\n\nOver the past few quarters, Apple has repeatedly warned that rising component costs would put pressure on its profit margins. Last quarter, gross margin was 50.1%, up from 49.3% in Q2. However, that included a roughly two-percentage-point benefit from tariff refunds.\n\nToday, Apple reported that its gross margin fell to 47.9% in Q4 2026, with product gross margin dropping to 37.2%, down from 40.1% in the previous quarter. That represented a 2.2-percentage-point decline in company-wide gross margin and a 2.9-percentage-point drop in product gross margin.\n\nAgainst the backdrop of record September quarter revenue of $114.5 billion, Apple CFO Kevan Parekh explained that tariff refunds once again provided some relief, though not enough to offset the impact of rising memory costs. He also noted that, excluding the impact of tariff refunds, the sequential decline in gross margins would have been roughly one percentage point, primarily due to higher memory costs:\n\n> “We saw strong performance in many services categories with all-time records in video, cloud services, payment services, and advertising, and a September quarter record in music. Company gross margin was 47.9%, and products gross margin was 37.2%. These both included a benefit from tariff refunds, which had a favorable impact of approximately 1 percentage point in the September quarter. When you remove the tariff refunds from both the June and September quarters, both company and product gross margin would be down about one point sequentially, primarily driven by higher memory costs.”\n\nParekh added that the pressure on Apple’s margins isn’t expected to ease anytime soon, with the company forecasting gross margins of between 45% and 46% for Q1 2027.\n\nHe attributed the expected decline primarily to higher memory costs, alongside the impact of the ongoing Siri AI rollout.\n\nWhen asked to elaborate, Parekh explained that Siri AI will affect Apple’s margins in two ways. First, running the service will increase cloud costs. Second, Apple will have to spread out the recognition of some revenue from devices that include Siri AI over their lifetimes, rather than counting it all at the time of sale.\n\nThis, he added, is an accounting practice Apple already follows for other services bundled with its devices, such as Maps, Siri, and iCloud:\n\n> “Consistent with how we’ve always accounted for Maps, Siri, and iCloud, for the devices we sell that include these bundled services, we defer a portion of the revenue and recognize it over the life of the device.”\n\nMeanwhile, CEO John Ternus described the current memory pricing situation as “unprecedented,” adding that Apple expects the cost of purchasing memory components to continue rising beyond the December quarter.\n\nTernus said recent price increases across the Mac, iPad, and iPhone lineups would help offset some of those costs, alongside existing inventory purchased at lower prices and savings on certain non-memory components. He also warned that the benefits of carrying lower-cost memory inventory would diminish over time. Apple did not say whether it expects to raise product prices yet again to compensate.\n\nFor the full breakdown of Apple’s Q4 2026 results, follow this link.","highlights":["Meanwhile, CEO John Ternus described the current memory pricing situation as “unprecedented,” adding that Apple expects the cost of purchasing memory components to continue rising beyond the December quarter."],"summary":"Apple Q4 2026 earnings call (Nov 2, 2026) – management commentary and December quarter outlook\n\n- Memory costs: Apple reports “unprecedented” memory pricing, expecting continued rise in memory component costs beyond Q1 FY27 (December quarter).\n- Impact on margins: Higher memory costs and Siri AI investments are anticipated to weigh on holiday-quarter profit margins.\n- Outlook: Management signals weaker margin pressure into the December quarter due to ongoing memory cost headwinds and continued AI/Siri-related investments, while product demand and revenue trajectory remain factors to watch.\n- Siri/AI investments: Ongoing AI initiatives (Siri) are contributing to operating costs, affecting near-term profitability despite potential long-term benefits.\n\nIf you want, I can tailor a tighter bullet summary around the exact figures or provide a stock-market impact view.","image":"https://9to5mac.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/04/Analysts-believe-Apple-taking-a-highly-unusual-step-to-double-Mac-user-base.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&resize=1200,628"}],"searchTime":3824.6,"costDollars":{"total":0.012,"search":{"neural":0.007},"summary":0.005},"warnings":[{"code":"IGNORED_FIELD","path":"/contents/highlights/highlightsPerUrl","message":"contents.highlights.highlightsPerUrl is no longer supported and is ignored.
